item.title: Features
item.description:
“PostgreSQL In Great STYle”: Postgres, Infras, Graphics, Service, Toolbox, it’s all Yours.

—— Battery-included, local-first PostgreSQL distribution, open-source RDS alternative

Value Propositions

  • Extensibility: Powerful extensions out of the box: deep integration of PostGIS, TimescaleDB, Citus, PGVector, 600 plugins, and 12 PG kernels.
  • Reliability: Quickly create high-availability, self-healing PostgreSQL clusters with built-in point-in-time recovery, access control, a self-signed CA, and TLS.
  • Observability: Prometheus and Grafana provide a modular monitoring stack that can operate independently. See the Gallery and Demo.
  • Availability: Deliver stable, reliable, auto-routed, transaction-pooled, read-write separated high-performance database services, with flexible access modes via HAProxy, Pgbouncer, and VIP.
  • Maintainability: Easy to use, Infrastructure as Code, Management SOPs, auto-tuning, local software repository, Vagrant sandbox and OpenTofu templates, zero-downtime migration solutions.
  • Composability: Modular architecture design, reusable Infra, various optional modules: Redis, Silo object storage, ETCD, DuckDB, Docker, Supabase.

Overview

Pigsty is a local, open-source alternative to PostgreSQL RDS:

item.title: RPO Trade-offs
item.description:
RPO (Recovery Point Objective) defines the maximum amount of data loss allowed when the primary fails.

Critical data, such as financial transactions, typically requires RPO = 0: no data loss.

Stricter RPO targets increase write latency and reduce throughput. Replica failure can also make the primary unavailable. Some workloads accept limited data loss for higher performance and availability.

Trade-offs

Asynchronous replicas normally lag behind the primary by about 10KB–100KB or 100µs–10ms, depending on network and throughput. At primary failure, a replica might not have received the latest data. Promotion can lose those unreplicated changes.

item.title: History
item.description:
Historical Origins

Pigsty began in 2018-2019 at Tantan. Tantan is a dating app similar to Tinder in China, later acquired by Momo. Its founding engineering team was Swedish, and its startup culture followed a Nordic model.

Tantan used PostgreSQL and Go as its core stack. Its architecture followed Instagram and centered on PostgreSQL. It served several million daily active users, millions of TPS, and hundreds of TB of data. The data layer used only PostgreSQL. PG stored procedures implemented almost all business logic, including 100ms recommendation algorithms. This was arguably one of China’s most complex large-scale PostgreSQL deployments at the time.

item.title: Get Started
item.description:
Use this guide to install Pigsty on one Linux node. Start with Quick Start. A node with 1 CPU core and 2 GB of memory is sufficient.

You can use a Linux MiniPC, a cloud server, Windows WSL, or a virtual machine on your laptop. Pigsty supplies Vagrant templates for local virtual machines. It also supplies OpenTofu templates for cloud servers.

The single-node installation includes these features:

  • 600 PostgreSQL extensions.
  • Grafana and Victoria monitoring services.
  • Infrastructure as code for deployment.
  • Local point-in-time recovery (PITR).

External object storage can keep PostgreSQL backups outside the node. These backups improve data durability for demonstrations, personal websites, and small services. A single node cannot provide high availability. Automatic failover requires at least three nodes.

item.title: Roadmap
item.description:
Release Strategy

Pigsty uses semantic versioning: <major>.<minor>.<patch>. Alpha/Beta/RC versions will have suffixes like -a1, -b1, -c1 appended to the version number.

Major versions introduce incompatible foundational changes and major features. Minor versions usually add features and small API changes. Patch versions provide bug fixes and package updates.

Pigsty plans one major release per year and usually 4-6 minor releases. Minor releases generally follow PostgreSQL minor releases within one month. See Release Notes for the full history.

item.title: Subscription

Pigsty combines tools from the PostgreSQL ecosystem with automated database management. It helps users use PostgreSQL, the world’s most popular database.

Pigsty resolves many PostgreSQL operational issues. Enterprise service quality also requires expert support and full coverage from the original provider. Pigsty Enterprise Edition adds these commercial services to the open-source edition. Choose services that meet your needs.

item.title: FAQ
item.description:
What is Pigsty, and what is it not?

Pigsty is a PostgreSQL distribution and a local-first, open-source RDS solution. It provides tools and operational practices for managing a DBMS. It is not itself a Database Management System (DBMS).

For comparison, a database is a car, a DBA is its driver, and RDS is a taxi service. Pigsty provides software to automate driving.

What problem does Pigsty solve?

Database operational expertise is scarce. Users can hire experts, rent managed RDS, or use Pigsty to automate database management. Pigsty helps users build efficient, high-quality local database services without a DBA, at less than 1/10 the cost of RDS.

item.title: Architecture
item.description:
Pigsty uses a modular architecture and declarative interface. Combine modules to meet your requirements.

  • Use one or more modules from the modular design.
  • Describe the environment with a configuration inventory and parameters. Apply it with Ansible playbooks.
  • Run Pigsty on physical or virtual nodes with a compatible OS.

Modules

Pigsty uses a modular design with infrastructure commonly assembled from these six modules: PGSQL, INFRA, NODE, ETCD, REDIS, and MINIO.

  • PGSQL: Self-healing HA Postgres clusters powered by Patroni, Pgbouncer, HAproxy, PgBackrest, and more.
  • INFRA: Local software repo, Nginx, Grafana, Victoria, AlertManager, Blackbox Exporter—the complete observability stack.
  • NODE: Tune nodes to desired state—hostname, timezone, NTP, ssh, sudo, haproxy, docker, vector, keepalived.
  • ETCD: Distributed key-value store as DCS for HA Postgres clusters: consensus leader election/config management/service discovery.
  • REDIS: Redis / Valkey servers supporting standalone primary-replica, sentinel, and cluster modes with full monitoring.
  • MINIO: Silo-backed S3-compatible object storage that can serve as an optional backup destination for PG databases.

Additional extension and pilot modules include DOCKER, JUICE, VIBE, KAFKA, and MYSQL. See Modules for deployment status and maturity.

item.title: ER Model
item.description:
A deployment is the largest entity in Pigsty. This entity-relationship diagram shows its main entities and their relationships:

A deployment is also an environment. Examples include Production (Prod), User Acceptance Testing (UAT), Staging, Testing, and Development (Devbox). Each environment has a Pigsty inventory that describes all its entities and attributes.

An environment usually has shared infrastructure (INFRA). This includes ETCD for the HA DCS and MINIO for centralized backup storage. Infrastructure serves multiple PostgreSQL clusters and other database modules. Deployments without infrastructure are also possible.

item.title: Infra as Code
item.description:
Pigsty uses IaC and GitOps. Describe the environment in a declarative inventory. Apply it with idempotent playbooks.

Declare the target state with parameters. Playbooks can repeatedly adjust nodes to that state. This resembles Kubernetes CRDs and Operators, implemented through Ansible on physical servers and VMs.

Pigsty was designed to manage large PostgreSQL deployments. Its target was to reproduce more than 100 database clusters, PG/Redis services, and monitoring on prepared servers within ten minutes. Manual GUI operations cannot complete that work in the available time. CLI-based IaC provides precise, efficient control.

item.title: Deployment
item.description:
Production deployments require Architecture Planning and Preparation beyond the Getting Started procedure. This chapter describes the complete deployment process and recommended practices for production.

Before production deployment, test the workflow in the Pigsty Sandbox. Use Vagrant to create a local 4-node sandbox. Use OpenTofu to create a larger simulation environment in the cloud.

Production high availability typically requires at least three nodes. Review the core Concepts and common administration procedures before deployment. These procedures include Configuration, Ansible Playbooks, and Security Hardening for enterprise compliance.

item.title: High Availability
item.description:
Overview

Pigsty PostgreSQL clusters include HA through Patroni, Etcd, and HAProxy.

A cluster with two or more instances gains automatic HA without extra configuration. A surviving instance can provide the complete database service. Clients can connect through any cluster node without tracking primary-replica changes.

Default norm mode targets RTO below 45 seconds. With asynchronous replication, pg_rpo=1MiB limits sampled lag for failover candidates. It does not bound actual data loss. Strict synchronous mode with crit.yml gives acknowledged transactions RPO = 0 during failover. Configure these settings for your hardware and reliability requirements.

item.title: RTO Trade-offs
item.description:
RTO (Recovery Time Objective) defines the maximum time required for the system to restore write capability when the primary fails.

Critical transaction systems typically need the shortest practical RTO, often below one minute.

Shorter RTO increases false failover risk. Network jitter can appear to be a failure. Cross-datacenter or cross-region deployments often allow 1–2 minutes to reduce this risk.

Trade-offs

pg_rto controls the failover unavailability limit. Presets fast, norm, safe, and wide support different network and deployment conditions. The default is norm, approximately 45 seconds.

item.title: Inventory
item.description:
Each Pigsty deployment has an inventory that describes the infrastructure and database clusters.

Configuration File

By default, Pigsty uses Ansible YAML configuration format. The inventory is a single file, pigsty.yml.

~/pigsty
 ^---- pigsty.yml # <---- Default configuration file

Edit this file to customize the deployment. Alternatively, use the configure wizard to generate it automatically.

Configuration Structure

The inventory uses Ansible YAML configuration format. It contains global parameters in all.vars and groups in all.children.

item.title: Configure
item.description:
The configure configuration wizard generates pigsty.yml for your current environment.

This script is optional. If you know how to configure Pigsty, edit pigsty.yml directly and skip the wizard.

Quick Start

Enter the Pigsty source directory and run ./configure to start the wizard. Without arguments, it uses the meta single-node template:

cd ~/pigsty
./configure # Interactive configuration wizard, auto-detect environment and generate config

The command starts with the selected template. It detects the current node IP address and region, then generates pigsty.yml for that environment.

item.title: Parameters
item.description:
Use inventory parameters to customize infrastructure settings and database configuration.

Parameter List

The current source and reference pages list 373 public parameters across 10 official modules. See Reference - Parameter List for the complete list. The native MySQL 8.4 pilot module has 13 additional public parameters. They are listed separately and excluded from this total.

Module Groups Params Description
PGSQL 9 124 PostgreSQL high-availability cluster configuration
INFRA 10 73 Software repositories and Victoria observability infrastructure
NODE 11 73 Node initialization, system tuning, and operations baseline
ETCD 2 13 ETCD cluster and removal protection parameters
MINIO 2 22 Silo deployment, observability, and removal parameters
REDIS 2 22 Redis/Valkey deployment and removal parameters
DOCKER 1 8 Docker engine parameters
JUICE 1 2 JuiceFS instance and cache parameters
VIBE 1 18 Code/Jupyter/Node.js/Claude/Codex configuration
KAFKA 2 18 Kafka deployment and removal-protection parameters

Parameter Form

Parameters are key-value pairs that describe entities. A key is a string. A value can be a boolean, string, number, array, or object.

item.title: Conf Templates
item.description:
The inventory defines the deployment through declarative configuration. Customize its pigsty.yml file for your requirements.

New users can start with ready-to-use templates for common deployment scenarios.

Each template is a predefined pigsty.yml file with defaults for a specific scenario.

Select a template, then change it to meet your requirements.

Using Templates

The optional configure wizard generates an inventory from your environment and input, with suitable defaults.

Use ./configure -c <conf> to select a template. <conf> is relative to conf; the .yml suffix is optional. Development sources move kernel templates to conf/fork/, selected with -c fork/<name>. Use the actual path in your source tree.

item.title: Use CMDB as Config Inventory
item.description:
Use a PostgreSQL metabase as a dynamic configuration source instead of static YAML files.

Overview

A CMDB (Configuration Management Database) stores configuration in database tables.

By default, Pigsty uses static pigsty.yml as the Ansible inventory.

A static file is simple. Larger deployments can need finer control, concurrent editing, and external integration beyond one file’s practical limits.

Feature Static YAML File CMDB Metabase
Querying Manual search/grep SQL queries with any conditions, aggregation analysis
Versioning Depends on Git or manual backup Database transactions, audit logs, time-travel snapshots
Access Control File system permissions, coarse-grained PostgreSQL fine-grained access control
Concurrent Editing Requires file locking or merge conflicts Database transactions naturally support concurrency
External Integration Requires YAML parsing Standard SQL interface, easy integration with any language
Scalability Difficult to maintain when file becomes too large Scales to physical limits
Dynamic Generation Static file, changes require manual application Immediate effect, real-time configuration changes

The sample pg-meta.meta database baseline defines the CMDB schema.

item.title: Security and Compliance
item.description:
Databases usually store the most valuable and sensitive data in an information system. Attacks and failures can therefore have severe consequences. Security requires multiple controls: who can connect, what they can do, and whether traffic is protected. It must also record operations and support recovery of damaged, lost, or deleted data.

Pigsty provides a default security baseline through declarative configuration. Declare HBA rules, roles and privileges, certificates, encryption, backups, and audit policies as parameters in the inventory. Idempotent playbooks render and apply these settings.

item.title: Security Model
item.description:
Identify the root of trust and defensive layers before selecting security features. The root of trust needs the strongest protection. Multiple layers preserve some protection if one fails.

Trust Boundaries

Pigsty uses Ansible for declarative deployment. Its administration node is the control plane and needs the strongest protection.

Role Assets and Privileges
Admin node The pigsty.yml inventory, which normally contains system and application credentials; the CA private key; SSH administration access to every node
INFRA nodes Monitoring and alerts, DNS, Nginx ingress, and software repositories
Database nodes Database instances, local dbsu, and restricted sudo
Clients Database credentials or client certificates; access through service ports, HBA, and authentication

These roles have different capabilities, not a simple hierarchy. Protect these three assets in particular:

item.title: Authentication
item.description:
pg_hba.conf defines PostgreSQL Host-Based Authentication. It controls who can connect, the source address, the database, and the required identity check.

Manual HBA maintenance across a cluster requires care. Primary and replica rules can differ, and each instance stores its configuration in its data directory. Without a shared declaration and refresh process, instance rules can diverge.

Pigsty declares HBA rules in the inventory through declarative configuration. Playbooks render and distribute them consistently.

item.title: Access Control
item.description:
Authentication verifies identity. Authorization determines what that identity can do.

PostgreSQL GRANT and REVOKE provide precise control. Privilege problems usually arise from missing default conventions. Examples include making an application account the owner, retaining temporary superuser access after troubleshooting, and omitting grants on new tables.

Pigsty provides four role tiers, default privileges, and database isolation. This starting model reduces manual grants per database. Operators must still assign roles to match business boundaries and regularly review effective privileges.

item.title: Encrypted Communication
item.description:
TLS can provide transport encryption, server authentication, and client authentication. Configure each protection separately. Enabling server TLS does not make clients verify the server or make the server require client certificates.

Most TLS operational work involves certificate issuance, distribution, trust, and rotation. Without central management, services often skip verification or keep plaintext connections.

Pigsty manages PKI declaratively. Deployment creates a local self-signed CA, issues component certificates, and distributes trust. TLS is then ready for use.

item.title: Data Security
item.description:
Network boundaries, authentication, and access control reduce incident risk. Data controls must limit damage and support recovery after hardware failure, leaked credentials, or operator errors.

Data security must provide integrity, recoverability, confidentiality if copied, and records of what happened.

Integrity

Bad disk sectors, memory bit flips, and firmware defects can cause silent data corruption, with no immediate error. Pigsty enables pg_checksum: true by default. Initialization uses data-checksums. PostgreSQL calculates each page checksum on write and checks it on read.

item.title: Compliance
item.description:
Compliance requires continuous evidence of three elements:

  • Configuration: Security controls must be enabled. Pigsty directly provides configuration.
  • Process: The organization must establish access approval, change management, recovery exercises, and related procedures.
  • Evidence: Records must show that configuration and processes remain effective. The inventory, runtime logs, and monitoring system provide part of this evidence.

This page provides a pre-launch checklist and maps Pigsty capabilities to common compliance frameworks. These mappings support architecture and gap analysis. They are not an MLPS assessment, SOC 2 audit opinion, or legal advice.

item.title: Single-Node Installation
item.description:
This guide installs Pigsty on one Linux node. Single Node For production deployments with multiple nodes, use the Deployment Guide.

The procedure has three stages: Install, Configure, and Deploy.

Summary

Prepare a node with a supported operating system. Use an administration account with passwordless SSH and sudo access.

Select a download source and run its command:

pigsty.io (Global)
curl -fsSL https://repo.pigsty.io/get | bash
pigsty.cc (China)
curl -fsSL https://repo.pigsty.cc/get | bash

The installation script downloads and extracts Pigsty into your home directory. It also installs the deployment dependencies.

item.title: Docker Deployment
item.description:
Pigsty runs on native Linux. It can also run in Linux containers with systemd. If you use macOS or Windows, use Docker to try a local single-node installation.

Quick Start

Enter the docker/ source directory. Run the launch command:

cd ~/pigsty/docker
make launch # Start container + generate config + deploy

item.title: Web Interface
item.description:
The default single-node installation includes the INFRA module. This module installs an Nginx web server on the node. Nginx supplies the Web UI and proxies requests to the monitoring services and other component interfaces.

Access

Enter the deployment node IP address in your browser. By default, Nginx uses port 80 for HTTP and port 443 for HTTPS. Replace 10.10.10.10 in these examples with your node IP address.

item.title: Customize Pigsty with Configuration
item.description:
You can generate a configuration file with the configuration wizard. You can also write the file yourself. This guide builds an inventory in stages.

The deploy.yml playbook deploys NODE, INFRA, ETCD, MINIO, and PGSQL when the inventory defines them. Docker, Redis, Kafka, native MySQL, JUICE, and VIBE require their own playbooks. The procedures below show the configuration and playbooks for each stage.

Minimal Configuration

The smallest valid configuration defines admin_ip. This is the IP address of the administration node where you installed Pigsty:

item.title: Run Playbooks with Ansible
item.description:
Pigsty uses Ansible to deploy and manage clusters. Ansible applies declarative configuration through playbooks. Pigsty module playbooks use idempotent tasks to reach the specified configuration.

For a single-node installation, use deploy.yml. Other built-in playbooks perform specific module operations. Ansible knowledge helps you manage Pigsty, but the single-node procedure does not require it.

Deploy Playbook

The deploy.yml playbook applies the core deployment configuration. It includes the CA, software repository, NODE, INFRA, ETCD, PGSQL, and MINIO when the inventory enables them. Optional modules such as Redis, Kafka, and native MySQL require their own playbooks. Defining these optional modules in the inventory does not add them to deploy.yml.

item.title: Offline Installation
item.description:
Pigsty normally installs packages from upstream Internet repositories. If the environment has no Internet access, use offline packages.

Overview

An offline package contains the RPM or DEB packages and dependencies from a local APT or YUM repository. It records the repository contents after an online installation.

Use offline packages for production deployments when you need consistent package versions. They let new nodes use the same packages as the existing nodes. They also remove the installation dependency on upstream repository availability.

item.title: Slim Installation
item.description:
Use Slim Installation to deploy PostgreSQL without the monitoring infrastructure. It installs ETCD, PGSQL, and part of NODE. It does not install INFRA, monitoring services, or a local software repository.

When to use Slim Installation
  • You only need PostgreSQL.
  • You have limited CPU or memory resources.
  • You already have an external monitoring system.
  • You do not need Grafana dashboards.

On one node, the omitted infrastructure uses approximately 0.2 vCPU and 500 MB of memory.

item.title: Security Recommendations
item.description:
The default configuration supports local demonstrations and development on a trusted intranet. If other hosts can reach the deployment, examine the credentials, network access, and sensitive files.

For production, also review the Security Model, Compliance, and Security Considerations.

Passwords

Pigsty publishes its default credentials in the source code and documentation. Do not use these credentials in production.

Run the configuration wizard with -g to generate random passwords:

./configure -g

The wizard replaces the built-in parameters and example credentials that it recognizes. It does not replace these credentials:

item.title: Concepts
item.description:
Pigsty is a portable, extensible, open-source PostgreSQL distribution. It uses declarative configuration and automation to build production database services in local environments. Its tools, scripts, and operating practices support PostgreSQL services at enterprise RDS levels.

Pigsty means PostgreSQL In Great STYle. It also means Postgres, Infras, Graphics, Service, Toolbox, it’s all Yours. It provides self-hosted PostgreSQL with graphical monitoring. Find source code on GitHub and information in the official documentation. Try the Web UI in the online demo.

item.title: Install Pigsty for Production
item.description:
This guide describes production deployment on multiple nodes. For single-node demonstrations or development, use Getting Started.

Summary

  1. Prepare the nodes according to your architecture plan.
  2. Install a supported Linux operating system.
  3. Configure SSH access.
  4. Use an administration account with passwordless ssh and sudo access.
  5. Run the installation command:
curl -fsSL https://repo.pigsty.io/get | bash; # International
curl -fsSL https://repo.pigsty.cc/get | bash; # Backup Mirror

The installation script downloads and extracts Pigsty into your home directory. It also installs the dependencies. Then complete configuration and deployment.

item.title: Prepare Resources for Serious Deployment
item.description:
Pigsty runs on nodes, which can be physical machines or virtual machines. This document describes the planning and preparation for deployment.

Node

Pigsty runs on the Linux kernel with x86_64 or aarch64 architecture. A node supplies a bare Linux operating system that you can access through SSH. It can be a physical machine, virtual machine, or container with systemd support. The node must have systemd, sudo, and sshd.

item.title: Planning Architecture and Nodes
item.description:
Pigsty uses a modular architecture. Select the modules for your requirements and define the deployment through declarative configuration.

Common Patterns

Use these common deployment patterns as a starting point. Adjust the configuration for your requirements:

Pattern INFRA ETCD PGSQL MINIO Description
Single-node (meta) 1 1 1 Single-node deployment default
Slim deploy (slim) 1 1 Database only, no monitoring infra
Infra-only (infra) 1 Monitoring infrastructure only
Rich deploy (rich) 1 1 1 1 Single-node + object storage + local repo with all extensions
Multi-node Pattern INFRA ETCD PGSQL MINIO Description
Two-node (dual) 1 1 2 Semi-HA, tolerates specific node failure
Three-node (trio) 3 3 3 3 Three-node HA, Silo EC:1
Four-node (full) 1 1 1+3 Demo setup, single INFRA/ETCD
Production simulation (simu) 3 5 9 4 20 nodes, including 2 additional proxies
Large-scale (custom) 3 5 n n 3 INFRA, 5 ETCD

Select the architecture for your reliability requirements and available resources. Production deployments with full high availability require at least 3 nodes. With 2 nodes, use the Semi-HA configuration.

item.title: Setup Admin User and Privileges
item.description:
Pigsty uses an operating system administration account with SSH and sudo access to every managed node. The account must be able to log in through SSH and run sudo commands on these nodes. Passwordless access is the standard configuration; password prompts are also supported.

User

Use an account name such as dba or admin. Avoid root and postgres:

  • You can deploy as root, but this is not recommended for production.
  • Do not use postgres (pg_dbsu) as the administration account.

Passwordless

You can enter passwords for each ssh and sudo command instead of configuring passwordless access. When you run playbooks, use -k|--ask-pass for the SSH password prompt. Use -K|--ask-become-pass for the sudo password prompt:

OpenTofu is an open-source infrastructure-as-code tool. It creates public cloud virtual machines from configuration files.

item.title: Security Considerations
item.description:
Pigsty defaults support development, testing, and demonstrations on a trusted intranet. For production, configure credentials, network boundaries, authentication, certificates, backups, and audit controls for your threat model.

Security and Compliance describes the mechanisms and their limits. Use the Launch Hardening Checklist for executable checks. The ha/safe template is a hardening example. Review each control for your environment before you use it.

item.title: FAQ
item.description:
What components are included in the INFRA module?

The current infra role directly manages these components:

  • Nginx: Exposes Grafana, VictoriaMetrics (VMUI), Alertmanager, and other WebUIs, and hosts local YUM/APT repositories.
  • DNSMasq: Provides DNS registration and resolution.
  • VictoriaMetrics suite: VictoriaMetrics, VMAlert, VictoriaLogs, and VictoriaTraces.
  • Alertmanager, Blackbox Exporter, and Grafana: Alert dispatch, blackbox probing, and visualization.

infra.yml also runs the CA, repository, NODE, HAProxy, and node-monitoring roles. These configure supporting services such as the self-signed CA, Chronyd, Node Exporter, and Vector on Infra nodes.

item.title: FAQ
item.description:
What is etcd’s role in Pigsty?

etcd is a distributed, reliable key-value store for critical system data. Pigsty uses etcd as the DCS (Distributed Config Store) for Patroni. It stores PostgreSQL HA status.

Patroni uses etcd for cluster failure detection, automatic failover, primary-replica switchover, and cluster configuration management.

etcd is critical for PostgreSQL HA. Its own availability requires a reachable majority. Production deployments normally put three or five voting members in independent failure domains.
